title: Comparing animals: fur, feathers, scales and legs
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 2 Biology, Comparing animals (Unit 4.1): how animals are similar and different, what makes a mammal or a bird, counting legs. Goes wider: fish, reptiles, amphibians and minibeasts, backbones, animals that break the rules, and many ways to sort. No textbook needed.
summary: A bat flies, but a bat is not a bird. Scientists sort animals by their bodies, not by what they do. Your child looks closely at a crow, a dog, an ant, a gecko and a fish, and says how they are alike and different. They feel their own hair and backbone, study a feather with a hand lens, count the legs of small animals at home and make a block graph. They learn what makes a mammal, a bird, a fish, a reptile, an amphibian and an insect. Then they meet animals that break the rules: a bird that can't fly, a mammal that lays eggs, and the flying fox, a bat. Last, they find that every animal in a group is still one of a kind.
builds_on: Class 1: living and non-living things and the signs of life. Class 1 and 3 plants rungs: plants are living things too. In Class 3 your child learns to sort all living things, plants and animals, into groups using questions and keys, meets the tree of life and finds out why scientists keep changing the groups. In Class 4 they go on a nature trail to study how animals' features suit their lives and how all living things depend on each other.
goals: By the end your child can say two ways two animals are alike and two ways they are different.
By the end your child can name the features of mammals (hair, milk) and birds (feathers, beaks, eggs with hard shells).
By the end your child can sort animals into mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, amphibians and insects, and say one feature of each.
By the end your child can count the legs of small animals and show the results on a block graph.
By the end your child can explain why a bat is a mammal and a penguin is a bird.
By the end your child can sort the same animals in two different ways and say that each animal is also unique.
words: a part or quality of an animal you can notice, like fur, wings or six legs
an animal with hair or fur that feeds their babies on milk. You are one.
an animal with feathers, a beak and wings, which lays eggs with hard shells
an animal that lives in water, breathes with gills and usually has scales and fins
an animal with dry, scaly skin, like a lizard, snake, turtle or crocodile
an animal like a frog that starts life in water and has soft, damp skin
a small animal with six legs and three body parts
the row of bones down the middle of your back
a chart made of blocks, one block for each thing counted
subconcepts: features we can observe: body covering, legs, wings, how babies begin
mammals: hair or fur, and milk for babies
birds: feathers, beaks, wings and hard-shelled eggs
small animals without a backbone: insects have 6 legs, spiders 8
counting legs and making a block graph
animals with and without a backbone
groups depend on bodies, not on what animals do (bats, whales, penguins)
animals that break the rules (the platypus)
the same animals can be sorted in many ways

days.title: Crow, dog, ant
days.goal: Notice how animals are alike and different, and sort them the child's own way.

steps.title: Who did you see today?
steps.do: Ask your child to name every animal they have seen this week: crows, pigeons, dogs, cats, cows, ants, flies, mosquitoes, a gecko on the wall, a fish, a cockroach. Write each name on a slip of paper. Then ask: 'Is a person an animal?' Accept any answer. You will come back to it on Day 7.

steps.title: Compare a crow and a dog
steps.do: From a window, a balcony or the street, watch a crow (or a pigeon) and a dog (or a cat or a cow) for a few minutes. Keep a safe distance. Ask: 'How are they alike?' (Both have eyes, a mouth and legs. Both breathe, eat and move. Both have a backbone.) 'How are they different?' (Feathers or fur. Two legs or four. A beak, or a mouth with teeth. Wings or no wings. A crow lays eggs, and a dog has puppies.) Write two ways they are alike and two ways they differ in a notebook, in your child's words.

steps.title: Sort them your way
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Spread out the animal slips. Ask your child to sort them into groups in any way they like. There is no wrong answer. They might choose 'flies or doesn't fly', 'big or small', 'lives with us or wild'. Ask them to name each group. Then mix them up and ask: 'Can you sort them a different way?' Say: 'Scientists sort animals too. This week we will find out how they do it, and why.'

steps.title: One of a kind
steps.do: Ask: 'Are all the crows on our street the same?' Look at two if you can. Say: 'Scientists have found that crows can tell people's faces apart. They remember a person who scared them. Every crow is different too, if we look closely. "Crow" is a useful name for the group, but each crow is still one of a kind.'

days.title: Mammals: fur and milk
days.goal: Find out what makes a mammal, and that we are mammals too.

steps.title: Your own fur
steps.do: Ask your child to find hair on their own body: on the head, the eyebrows, the eyelashes, and the tiny hairs on their arms. Look with a hand lens if you have one. Ask: 'Who else has hair or fur?' (Dogs, cats, cows, goats, monkeys, rats and squirrels. Elephants have a few stiff hairs. Many baby whales have a few whiskers.) 'What did you drink when you were a tiny baby?' (Milk.)

steps.title: What is a mammal?
steps.do: Say: 'Animals with hair or fur that feed their babies on milk are called mammals. The name comes from mamma, the Latin word for the breast, where the milk is made. You are a mammal. So are cows, goats, dogs, squirrels, bats, elephants and whales.' Ask: 'Which mammals give us milk?' (Cows, buffaloes, goats, camels, even yaks.) 'Who is that milk really for?' (Their own babies.)

steps.title: Story: The Flying Fox's Daughter
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Don't explain it. Then ask the story's questions, especially: 'Why did Kavya think the flying foxes were birds? What made her change her mind?'

steps.title: Mammal mime
steps.do: Take turns acting out a mammal while the other person guesses: a cow chewing, a monkey swinging, a bat hanging upside down, an elephant drinking with their trunk, a whale blowing out air. After each one, the guesser says how they know the animal is a mammal. Add one trick: act out a hen. Ask: 'Is a hen a mammal?' (No. A hen has feathers and lays eggs.)

steps.title: Mammals that fly and swim
steps.do: Ask: 'A bat flies. Is a bat a bird?' (No. Bats have fur, give birth to live babies and feed them milk. A bat is a flying mammal.) 'A whale swims. Is a whale a fish?' (No. A whale breathes air and feeds her baby milk. A whale is a swimming mammal.) Say: 'What an animal does does not decide their group. Their body does.'

need: a hand lens if you have one

days.title: Birds: feathers, beaks and eggs
days.goal: Investigate a feather and find out what makes a bird.

steps.title: Feather lab
steps.do: Do Experiment e1 with a clean feather. A pigeon feather from the balcony works well, washed in soapy water and dried. A craft feather from a stationery shop also works. Look at the feather with a hand lens, open and close the gaps between the barbs, wave it through the air, and drip water on it. Ask: 'What do you notice? What do you think feathers are for?'

steps.title: What is a bird?
steps.do: Say: 'Only birds have feathers. Every bird has feathers, a beak with no teeth, two legs and two wings. Every bird lays eggs with hard shells.' Ask: 'Do all birds fly?' (No. Ostriches, emus, penguins and kiwis can't fly. A penguin uses their wings to swim underwater.) Talk about the beaks of birds you know: a parrot's hooked beak cracks seeds, a sunbird's thin curved beak sips nectar from flowers, a crow's strong beak eats almost anything, and a duck's flat beak scoops food from water.

steps.title: Salim Ali's sparrow
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v2. About 120 years ago in Bombay (now Mumbai), a boy called Salim Ali shot a sparrow with an air gun. The sparrow had a yellow patch on the throat, and he wanted to know what kind of sparrow this was. He grew up to be India's best-known bird scientist. Ask the voice's question.

steps.title: Birds are dinosaurs
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v3. Say: 'Scientists now agree that birds are living dinosaurs. The pigeon on your balcony is a distant cousin of Tyrannosaurus.' Look at a pigeon's feet: they are covered in scales, like a lizard's skin. Ask the voice's question.

steps.title: Bird walk
steps.do: Stand at a window or on the balcony for a few minutes. Name or describe every bird you see or hear. For each bird, say one feature: beak shape, colour, size, or how the bird moves (hops, walks or flies).

need: a clean feather (washed and dried) or a craft feather
a dropper or spoon of water

days.title: Scales, gills and slimy skin
days.goal: Meet fish, reptiles and amphibians, and compare body coverings.

steps.title: Feel the coverings
steps.do: Ask your child to close their eyes. Let them touch a piece of wool (like a mammal's hair), a feather (a bird's covering), and the skin of a bitter gourd (bumpy, a little like a crocodile's skin). If you cook fish, add a fish scale. Ask them to guess each one and describe it: soft, smooth, rough or bumpy?

steps.title: Fish watch
steps.do: Look at a fish: in a home tank, a fish bought for cooking, or a short video of fish swimming. Find the fins for steering, the tail for pushing, the scales, and the flaps on each side of the head that open and close. Say: 'These flaps cover the gills. Water has a little air mixed into it. A fish takes in that air through their gills.' Ask: 'Does a fish have a backbone?' (Yes. Think of the long row of bones in a cooked fish.)

steps.title: Reptiles and amphibians
steps.do: Look at a house gecko (palli) on the wall. Say: 'Lizards, snakes, turtles and crocodiles are reptiles. They have dry skin covered in scales, and most lay eggs on land.' Then talk about frogs: 'A frog is an amphibian. The word means "two lives". A frog starts as an egg in water and hatches into a tadpole, who breathes with gills. The tadpole grows legs and loses the tail. The grown frog lives on land and in water and has soft, damp skin.' In the monsoon, if there is a pond nearby, look for tadpoles, but don't take them.

steps.title: Animal groups
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1. Read each question aloud. Your child answers, and you write the 'why' answers in their words.

need: wool, a feather, a bitter gourd, and a fish scale if you cook fish

days.title: How many legs?
days.goal: Find small animals at home, count their legs and make a block graph.

steps.title: Feel your backbone
steps.do: Your child bends forward while you run a finger gently down their back. Say: 'Feel the bumps? That is your backbone.' Then say: 'Mammals, birds, fish, reptiles and amphibians all have a backbone. Most kinds of animals in the world don't. Insects, spiders, worms, snails and crabs have no backbone.' Ask: 'How does an ant keep their shape with no bones inside?' (An ant has a hard outer skin, like armour.)

steps.title: Leg count at home
steps.do: Do Activity a2. For 10 minutes, look for small animals in the kitchen, near the windows, in corners and around potted plants. Ants, flies, mosquitoes, a house spider or a cockroach are nearly always there. Look, don't touch. Count each animal's legs, using a hand lens if you have one. Then add the animals from the Day 1 slips. Make a tally mark for each animal under 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 or many legs. Ants, flies, mosquitoes and cockroaches have 6 legs, so they are insects. Spiders have 8. Worms and fish have none.

steps.title: Make a block graph
steps.do: On squared paper, your child colours one square for each animal, in columns: no legs, 2 legs, 4 legs, 6 legs, 8 legs, many legs. Ask: 'Which column is tallest? Why do you think so?' Then say: 'If we counted every kind of animal in the world, the 6-legs column would be the tallest by far. Insects are the biggest group of animals. There are more kinds of beetle than kinds of mammal.'

steps.title: Is a spider an insect?
steps.do: Ask: 'A spider is small and has many legs. Is a spider an insect?' (No. A spider has 8 legs and 2 body parts, and no wings or feelers. Spiders belong to a group called arachnids, with scorpions and ticks.) Draw an ant and a spider side by side. Count their body parts and legs together.

days.title: Animals that break the rules
days.goal: Meet animals that don't fit the boxes, and see that every animal is one of a kind.

steps.title: The platypus puzzle
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v1, the platypus of Australia. The platypus has fur, a bill like a duck's and webbed feet. A mother platypus lays eggs, then feeds her babies milk. Show a picture. Ask: 'Is the platypus a mammal, a bird or something else?' (A mammal, because of the fur and the milk. The platypus is one of only five kinds of mammals that lay eggs.) Ask the voice's question.

steps.title: Animal Families
steps.do: Play the card game (g1). When someone asks for a card, they must say one feature of that group. Watch out for the trick cards (bat, whale, penguin, platypus, spider).

steps.title: Ten crows, all different
steps.do: Ask your child to draw ten crows (or ten ants, or ten cats) and make each one different: in size, pose, and what the crow is doing. Ask: 'They are all crows. Are they all the same?' Then ask: 'Are you the same as every other child? Is any group of animals really all the same?'

steps.title: Tricky animals
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2 together. Your child explains the tricky ones out loud before choosing.

need: a picture of a platypus (a book or a phone)

days.title: Animal museum and teach it back
days.goal: Show and explain what makes each animal group.

steps.title: Set up the museum
steps.do: Start the project. Make an animal museum on a table. Put out the feather, and a photo or drawing for each group: mammal, bird, fish, reptile, amphibian, insect and spider. Add the block graph and the ten-crows drawing. Your child writes or tells you a label for each: 'Mammals have…'

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child gives a museum tour to the family and explains the features of each group, why a bat is a mammal and a penguin is a bird, and what the block graph shows. Then ask the check questions.

steps.title: Is a person an animal?
steps.do: Go back to the question from Day 1. Ask: 'Is a person an animal? Which group are we in? What do we share with a crow, a fish and an ant?' (We are mammals. We share a backbone with the crow and the fish. With the ant we share breathing, eating, growing and having young.) Then ask: 'If an ant sorted animals, what groups would the ant make?'

steps.title: Animal puzzles
steps.do: Try Worksheet ws3 if your child wants more. Read each puzzle aloud.

sections.p: Match the group to its feature.
pairs: hair or fur, and milk for babies
starts life in water, soft damp skin

experiments.title: Feather lab
experiments.question: What is a feather like, and what can it do?
need: a clean feather (washed in soapy water and dried) or a craft feather
a dropper or spoon of water
steps: Look at the feather with the hand lens. Find the stiff middle stick, called the shaft, and the hundreds of thin barbs on each side.
Gently pull two barbs apart, so a gap appears. Then stroke the feather from the bottom to the tip between finger and thumb. Watch the gap close up again, like a zip.
Wave the feather fast through the air. Then wave a strip of paper the same size. Which pushes more air?
Drip a few drops of water on the feather. Watch where the drops go.
If you have a soft, fluffy feather too, compare the two. Which would keep a bird warm? Which would help a bird fly?
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will happen to the water? Can you break a feather by pulling it apart?'
experiments.observe: The barbs hook back together. The feather pushes more air than the paper. Water often stays in round drops and rolls off.
experiments.why: Each barb has even tinier branches with hooks, called barbules. They lock together like a zip. So the feather is light but makes a strong surface that pushes on the air. A bird zips their feathers back by pulling them through the beak. This is called preening. Many birds spread oil from near the tail onto their feathers, which helps water roll off. Fluffy down feathers trap warm air close to the body. Today only birds have feathers. Long ago, some other dinosaurs had them too.
experiments.safety: Use a washed feather or a craft feather, and wash hands afterwards. Don't pick up feathers near sick or dead birds.

activities.title: Sort them your way
need: slips of paper with one animal name or drawing on each
a large space on the floor
steps: Spread the slips out face up.
Your child sorts them into groups however they like and names each group.
Ask why each animal went into that group.
Mix them up and ask for a completely different way of sorting.
Write down both ways. Compare them with the scientists' groups later in the week.
activities.outcome: Two or more ways of sorting the same animals, made by your child, showing that sorting depends on what you choose to look at.

activities.title: Leg count at home
need: a hand lens if you have one
steps: Look in the kitchen, near windows and lights, in corners and around potted plants. If you have a garden or a park nearby, look under flowerpots and leaves too.
Watch each animal without touching and count their legs. Count mosquitoes and cockroaches from a distance.
Make a tally mark in the right column: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 or many legs. Add a mark for each animal on the Day 1 slips too.
Leave every animal where you found them.
Count the tally marks in each column.
activities.outcome: A tally of animals by number of legs, ready to turn into a block graph.

project.title: Our animal museum
steps: Collect one object or picture for each group: mammal, bird, fish, reptile, amphibian, insect, spider.
Make a label for each: the group name and two features.
Add the trick animals: bat, whale, penguin and platypus. Each one gets a label saying why they belong in their group.
Add the block graph and the ten-crows drawing.
Give a tour to the family.
project.outcome: A table-top museum of animal groups, with labels written by your child.

game.title: Animal Families
rules: Cut out the cards. There are seven families of four: mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, amphibians, insects, and spiders with their cousins.
Shuffle and deal 5 cards each. Put the rest face down as a pile.
On your turn, ask another player for a card from a family you're collecting, and say one feature of that family: 'Do you have a mammal? Mammals have fur and milk.'
If they have one, they must give it to you. If not, take one from the pile.
When you have all four cards of a family, put them down. When the cards run out, the player with the most families wins.
Trick cards (bat, whale, penguin, platypus, spider) belong to a family too. When you put one down, say why the animal belongs there.

cards.back: amphibian: no legs! lives in soil

big: Who decided which groups animals go into? Could we have chosen different groups?
If every crow is different, what does it mean to call them all 'crows'?
What would an ant's way of sorting animals look like?

challenge.q: Bats are birds because they fly.
challenge.hint: No. Bats have fur, give birth to live babies and feed them milk, so they are mammals. Flying doesn't decide a group. Many insects fly too, and some birds can't. Ask: what is a group really based on?

challenge.q: Whales and dolphins are fish because they live in the sea.
challenge.hint: No: they breathe air through a blowhole, feed their babies milk and have a few hairs when young. They are mammals whose ancestors lived on land millions of years ago. Their closest living land cousin is the hippo.

challenge.q: All mammals give birth to live babies.
challenge.hint: Almost all. The platypus and the echidnas of Australia and New Guinea lay eggs, then feed their young milk. When the first platypus reached Britain in 1799, some scientists thought it was a fake. Ask: when an animal breaks a rule, should we change the animal's group or the rule?

perspectives.view: Scientists have found that crows can recognise individual human faces and remember people who were unkind to them for years. To a crow, we are not 'humans', we are this person and that person. Ask: how do you think the crows on your street sort the people they see?

A woman who herds fifty goats knows each goat by their face, voice and habits, and has a name for each one. To a visitor they are 'goats'. Ask: when is it useful to see a group, and when is it better to see each one?

Flying foxes hang upside down all day. At night they fly many kilometres to eat fruit, and they carry seeds and pollen from tree to tree. Many people are afraid of bats. Ask: what would a flying fox want people to know about them?

voices.who: The platypus puzzle: George Shaw (1751–1813) in London, and the Aboriginal peoples of Australia
voices.idea: In 1799 Shaw described a dried platypus skin sent from Australia. The animal had fur like an otter, a bill like a duck and webbed feet. Shaw wrote that it was hard not to suspect a trick. Some say he looked for stitches where a bill might have been sewn on. Later, scientists argued for decades over whether the platypus laid eggs.
voices.then: Aboriginal Australians had known the platypus, and known that she laid eggs, for thousands of years, but European scientists didn't ask them or didn't believe them. In 1884 a scientist, William Caldwell, finally confirmed the eggs.
voices.now: The platypus is accepted as a real mammal who has fur, makes milk and lays eggs. Platypuses belong to a small, ancient group of mammals called monotremes.
voices.ask: The people who lived alongside the platypus already knew the platypus laid eggs. Why do you think the scientists in faraway Britain took so long to find out? Who should they have asked?

voices.idea: As a boy, Salim Ali shot a sparrow with an air gun and noticed a yellow patch on the bird's throat. Curious, he took the bird to the Bombay Natural History Society, where W. S. Millard identified the bird as a yellow-throated sparrow and showed him the Society's collections of birds. Salim Ali went on to spend his life studying India's birds and wrote 'The Book of Indian Birds'.
voices.then: Few Indians worked as bird scientists then. He had no university degree in zoology, and for years he could not find a job studying birds.
voices.now: He is honoured as 'the Birdman of India'. His careful observations of how birds live, not just what they look like, are accepted. He later worked to protect birds and their homes, such as Bharatpur's wetlands.
voices.ask: Salim Ali began by shooting a bird and ended by protecting birds. Can a person change what they care about? What did his curiosity notice that others might have missed?

voices.who: John Ostrom (1928–2005), USA, and the idea that birds are dinosaurs
voices.idea: In 1969 Ostrom described Deinonychus, a fast, light dinosaur, and pointed out how much the dinosaur's skeleton was like a bird's. He argued that birds evolved from small meat-eating dinosaurs.
voices.then: Many scientists thought dinosaurs were slow, cold-blooded animals like giant lizards, and that birds came from some other reptile. His idea was doubted.
voices.now: Since the 1990s, many fossils of dinosaurs with feathers have been found, especially in China. Scientists now accept that birds are living dinosaurs. Exactly which dinosaurs could fly or glide, and how flight began, is still debated.
voices.ask: If birds are dinosaurs, are dinosaurs really extinct? Which is the right group for a pigeon: 'bird', 'dinosaur', or both?

story.title: The Flying Fox's Daughter
text: My family lives in the great banyan tree beside the old temple tank in the middle of the town. There are four hundred of us, maybe more. By day we hang from the branches, upside down, wrapped in our wings like folded umbrellas. We squabble and doze and lick our fur clean. By night we fly. We are flying foxes, a kind of bat. It is a funny name, because we are not foxes. Some people call us birds. That is where my story begins.

The girl who called us birds was named Kavya. She was eight. Every day she walked under our tree with her grandmother, who sold boiled peanuts from a cart at the edge of the tank. Kavya would stand with her head tipped back and her mouth open, looking up at us.
"Look at the big black birds, Paati," she would say. "Why do they sleep upside down?"
"They're not birds, kanna," her grandmother would say, counting change.
"They have wings," said Kavya. "They fly. They live in a tree. So they're birds." She was so sure that her grandmother only laughed.

I had a daughter that spring. She was born in the tree, in the middle of the day, and she came out of me already holding on: her tiny claws gripped my fur, and her mouth found my milk at once, under my wing. She was the size of a small mango, with soft grey fur and eyes that were not yet quite open. For the first weeks of her life she went everywhere with me, clinging to my chest as I flew out over the town each night to the fig and jamun trees by the river, and back again before dawn.

But babies grow heavy. One morning, as I landed in the banyan after a long night's flying, my daughter's grip slipped. She fell. She tumbled down through the leaves and the air roots, past my sisters and my aunts, and landed with a small thump on the ground beside the peanut cart, and lay there squeaking.
I screamed. All four hundred of us screamed. We do that when one of us is in trouble, and the noise is terrible. People ran out of the shops. Kavya dropped the paper cone of peanuts she was holding.
"A baby bird!" she cried, and she reached for my daughter.

"No!" said her grandmother, and she caught Kavya's hand. "Don't touch. Never touch a bat with your hands. The baby is frightened and may bite, and bats can carry sicknesses. And the mother is up there, watching. If we help, we help the right way."

Paati knew a woman who rescued animals. Everyone in the town did. Paati telephoned her. While they waited, she gently put an upturned basket over my daughter so that the crows could not get her. Then she and Kavya sat beside the basket, very still.
The rescuer came on a scooter with thick gloves and a soft towel. She lifted the basket, picked up my daughter carefully in the towel, and held her up so that Kavya could see.
Kavya leaned closer. And I saw her face change.

My daughter was not a bird. Anyone who looked at her properly could see it. She had no feathers at all. She had soft grey fur all over, like a kitten. She had no beak. She had a little fox-like face with a wet nose and a mouth full of tiny teeth, and she was opening it to call for me. Her wings were not made of feathers either. They were made of thin, warm skin, stretched between long, long fingers. And at the front of each wing was a thumb with a claw, gripping the towel.
"She's got fur," said Kavya slowly. "She's got teeth. She's got hands."
"She drinks milk from her mother," said the rescuer. "Just like a calf. Just like you did. She's a mammal, like you and me. Not a bird at all. A mammal who flies."
Kavya was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "So she's more like me than like a crow?"
"In lots of ways," said the rescuer, "yes."

The rescuer did what good rescuers do. She did not take my daughter away. She borrowed a ladder from a shop, climbed a little way up the banyan's great trunk, and wrapped the towel loosely around a low branch, with my daughter clinging to it, high enough to be safe from dogs. Then everyone went to the far side of the tank and waited.

I came down. I crept along the branch, upside down, the way we do, and my daughter smelled me and called, and I folded her into my wing, and she found my milk at once, and held on, and this time she did not let go.

Every day after that, Kavya stood under our tree and looked up. She didn't call us birds again. She called us by our proper name, flying foxes, and she told everyone who would listen that we had fur and milk and fingers in our wings, and that we were more like her than like a crow. Sometimes she even told them that every night we fly out over the town and come back with our faces dusted with pollen and our bellies full of figs, and drop the seeds of new trees wherever we go.
She was right about all of it. And I, who hang upside down in the banyan tree, I liked her very much for looking properly.
story.epiphany: A bat is not a bird. Bats have fur, teeth and finger bones in their skin wings, give birth to live babies and feed them milk, so bats are mammals. Groups are decided by bodies, not by what an animal does, such as flying. The turn is Kavya looking closely at the fallen baby in the towel and seeing fur, teeth and fingers instead of feathers and a beak. Looking closely showed her that a bat's body is more like hers than like a crow's.
ask: Why did Kavya think the flying foxes were birds?
What did she notice when she looked closely at the baby?
Why did Paati stop Kavya from touching the baby bat? What did they do instead?
How is a flying fox like you?
What does the mother bat mean when she says she liked Kavya 'for looking properly'?

ideas.idea: Groups are about bodies, not about what animals do.
ideas.more: A bat flies but is a mammal. A penguin can't fly but is a bird. A whale swims but breathes air and makes milk. Scientists group animals by features they share because they share ancestors. Ask your child to find a flying animal in every group they know.

ideas.idea: You are an animal, and a mammal.
ideas.more: You have hair, you drank milk, you have a backbone. You share these with cows, bats and whales, and you share breathing, eating and growing with every animal, even an ant.

ideas.idea: A group name is useful, but each animal is one of a kind.
ideas.more: Calling something 'a crow' helps us talk and think. But every crow is a particular crow, and crows can tell every human apart. Use the groups, then look past them.

unknowns: How many kinds of animals are there on Earth? Scientists have named about one and a half million kinds, mostly insects, but there may be several times more that nobody has named yet.
What is it like to be a bat, finding your way by the echoes of your own voice? A philosopher, Thomas Nagel, asked this in 1974. Nobody can answer it, because we can't get inside a bat's experience.
Why did the platypus and echidnas keep laying eggs when almost all other mammals stopped? Scientists have ideas but no certain answer.

check.q: Tell me two ways a crow and a dog are alike and two ways they are different.
check.a: Alike: both have a backbone, eyes, legs, breathe and eat. Different: feathers or fur, two or four legs, beak or teeth, eggs or puppies.

check.q: What makes an animal a mammal?
check.a: Hair or fur, and feeding their babies on milk.

check.q: What makes an animal a bird?
check.a: Feathers, a beak, wings, and eggs with hard shells.

check.q: How many legs does an insect have? A spider?
check.a: An insect has six legs. A spider has eight, so a spider is not an insect.

check.q: Why is a bat a mammal and not a bird?
check.a: A bat has fur and feeds her babies milk. Flying doesn't decide the group.
